title: Mary prays (CCC 2617–2619)

lines: A SHORT YES, A LONG SONG.
cards: Two scenes, close together in Luke's Gospel. In the first, a woman in Nazareth hears an angel's message that will rearrange her whole life, and she answers in one sentence.
In the second, she has walked into the hill country to see her cousin Elizabeth, and when Elizabeth greets her, she doesn't answer in one sentence. She sings. A short yes, and then a long song.

teach.h: BE IT DONE TO ME: FIAT.
teach.b: You've met both scenes before; today the Catechism reads them as prayer. The angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear a son. She asks how.
He answers. And she says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, that be it done is one word: fiat.
The Catechism says simply: this is Christian prayer, to be wholly God's, because he is wholly ours. It isn't a request. It's an offering.
She doesn't know what comes next, and she says yes anyway. Then the second prayer.

teach.h: MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.
teach.b: Elizabeth calls her blessed, and Mary answers: "My soul doth magnify the Lord. And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In Latin it begins Magnificat, and that's the song's name.

The Catechism calls it the song both of the Mother of God and of the Church. It sings that God has scattered the proud, put down the mighty, lifted up the lowly, and filled the hungry with good things.
Praise, in Mary's mouth, is not polite. It's a song about the world turned right side up.

teach.h: WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU.
teach.b: One more moment: at a wedding in Cana, when the wine runs out, Mary tells Jesus, then tells the servants, "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye."
The Catechism sees her there asking on behalf of others, and pointing them toward her Son. First yes, then praise, and all along, pointing past herself.

how: Catholics say Mary's fiat in the Angelus, where be it done unto me according to thy word is one of its lines, and the Magnificat is sung or said at Vespers, the evening prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours.

games.q: an angel tells you your whole life is about to change. you ask how. he answers. what do you say?
o: be it done to me according to thy word.
let me talk to my family.
games.why: Mary answers with her fiat: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."

practice: First the yes: bring to mind one thing you've been resisting, something you can't control, and without solving it, try letting it be; if you pray, borrow Mary's words, be it done to me according to thy word.
Then the praise: name, slowly, a few good things that are real today. If you don't pray, let yes and gladness simply sit side by side.

wordCard.voice: Mary prays. Her fiat at the Annunciation, be it done to me, and her Magnificat at the Visitation, my soul doth magnify the Lord: in Catholic teaching, yes to God, then praise. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: let it be done — Mary's answer in Luke 1:38, in the Vulgate.

carryVoice: Your line: yes, then praise. Her yes came before she knew what came next. See you tomorrow.
